item.title: Why People Deeply in Love Still Feel Romantic Temptation
item.description:
Relationships

Why People Deeply in Love Still Feel Romantic Temptation

Romantic temptation is not the opposite of love.

Posted June 20, 2026

Key points
  • Emotions arise when we perceive significant changes in our situation or in the lives of those close to us.
  • The opposite of love is not temptation but indifference.
  • Romantic temptation is a common emotional experience; acting on it is a separate behavioral choice.
  • People with high self-control proactively avoid tempting situations and need to resist temptation less often.

“Love me or hate me, but spare me your indifference.” — Libbie Fudim

If your partner admits finding someone else attractive, does that mean your relationship is in trouble? Many people think so. They assume that genuine love leaves no room for romantic temptation.

Psychology tells a different story. Feeling tempted is often perfectly compatible with deep commitment. Romantic temptation is therefore nearly universal; infidelity is not. The real opposite of love is not temptation—it is indifference. Love and temptation are both emotional attitudes that draw us toward another person. The difference lies not in their psychological mechanism but in how we evaluate and manage them.

What Is Romantic Temptation?

“Temptation in my heart, I'm burning, I fall apart! When the night falls, my heart calls for love and devotion.” — Arash & Rebecca

Temptation is the desire to do something that conflicts with one's values or commitments. Like other emotional attitudes, it arises automatically rather than by choice. What distinguishes temptation is not that it occurs but that it often challenges our long-term goals and profound commitments.

Romantic temptation generally takes two forms. Sexual temptation involves physical attraction, novelty, and desire. Emotional temptation involves feeling unusually understood, appreciated, or emotionally close to someone outside the relationship. While sexual temptation is more openly discussed—and condemned—emotional temptation can be equally powerful. Social media has multiplied opportunities for romantic temptation while making them easier to pursue.

Why Temptation Is Normal

“I generally avoid temptation unless I can't resist it.” — Mae West

Emotions arise when we perceive significant changes in our circumstances—or in the lives of people who matter to us. Like a burglar alarm, emotions signal that something deserves attention. Once no further action is needed, the signal fades (Ben-Ze'ev, 2000). Evolution has therefore made our emotional system especially responsive to novelty and change—which may either improve or threaten our well-being—rather than to stability.

Sexual desire is especially responsive to novelty. A well-known anecdote about President Calvin Coolidge illustrates this principle. While touring a government farm, the president and first lady were shown a rooster that mated repeatedly throughout the day. Mrs. Coolidge reportedly asked the guide to mention this to the president. Coolidge listened and asked, "Same hen every time?" "Oh no, Mr. President—a different hen each time." "Tell that to Mrs. Coolidge," he replied. This exchange gave its name to the Coolidge Effect--many mammals, including humans, show renewed sexual interest when presented with a novel partner.

article continues after advertisement

Commitment does not eliminate such responsiveness. Even happily partnered people continue noticing attractive, intelligent, or engaging alternatives. Confusing temptation with infidelity is like confusing anger with aggression: One is an emotional attitude, the other is a certain behavior that may, or may not, accompany the attitude. The important psychological question is not whether committed people experience temptation but how they respond to it.

What People Say About Romantic Temptation

Here is a sample of responses from women discussing romantic temptation on Reddit:

  • "Temptation is those random moments where you find someone attractive or feel a little spark, even though you're happy with your partner."
  • "When someone was trying to get to know me, I thought: why would I chase a spark when I already have a fire?"
  • "I've had crushes, and I know my husband has too. I'd never act on it. Commitment doesn't turn attraction off—it just changes what you do with it."
  • "Been together 17 years and have had a couple of crushes. But love is choosing your partner every day, even when it's not easy."
  • "We are married, not dead. It's only an issue if pursued—emotionally or physically."
  • "It's completely normal to become attracted to someone else while in a relationship. It's almost strange that anyone would see it as a sign of deeper depravity."

Preventing Temptation Is Easier than Resisting It

“Opportunity may knock only once, but temptation leans on the doorbell.” — Oprah Winfrey

Because temptation emerges automatically, successful relationships depend less on suppressing desire than on managing the situations in which desire develops. People manage temptation in two ways: resisting it once it appears or—more effectively—avoiding situations in which it is likely to develop.

article continues after advertisement

Research suggests that committed partners often rely on subtle, largely automatic strategies: viewing attractive alternatives less favorably, shifting attention away from potential rivals, and investing more deeply in their own relationship (McNulty et al., 2018). Adopting a broader perspective on one's life, family, and long-term goals reduces romantic interest in alternatives while strengthening commitment to one's partner (Birnbaum et al., 2024). Habitually devaluing attractive alternatives can both diminish their appeal and reinforce commitment (Lydon et al., 2026).

People with high self-control appear especially skilled at preventing temptation rather than fighting it after it has intensified. They proactively avoid situations likely to trigger conflict and, as a result, report resisting impulses less often than others (Ent et al., 2015). Enduring relationships depend less on heroic acts of willpower than on wise, everyday emotional regulation.

Does Temptation Mean the Relationship Is Unhappy?

“The road to success is dotted with many tempting parking spaces.” — Will Rogers

Experiencing romantic temptation does not necessarily signal dissatisfaction. Even people in deeply fulfilling relationships occasionally notice attractive alternatives. What distinguishes them is not the absence of temptation but the value they place on preserving their primary relationship.

Love does not eliminate competing possibilities. It simply changes which possibilities deserve to shape the future. The strongest relationships are not those in which temptation never appears but those in which commitment repeatedly outweighs temptation. Enduring love is measured less by what we occasionally feel than by what we consistently choose. Temptation is not the enemy of love. Indifference is.

item.title: When Healing Triggers Grief
item.description:
Grief

When Healing Triggers Grief

Why healing is not always the relief we expect it to be.

Posted June 20, 2026

Key points
  • Healing often feels better and worse at the same time.
  • Anger and sadness aren't detours; they're part of the process.
  • Healing begins when you stop fighting your emotions.

“Is it weird that I feel better and worse at the same time?”

“Huh?” I didn’t expect to hear that from my client, a 62-year-old man with whom I’d been working as a personal trainer.

“Physically, I feel like a million bucks. I’m stronger, and not as cranky.” He paused, holding the medicine ball I’d just handed him. “Then I think about how I should’ve started exercising when I was younger, and I get so mad. And sad. My life could’ve been so much better.”

I was a trainer, not a therapist, and I never knew how to handle these revelations. So, I did what I knew best. “Well, you’re here now, right? Come on, slam that medicine ball with everything you got, and don’t forget to engage your core.”

He laughed, shook his head. “You’re relentless, kid.”

How can someone feel better and worse at the same time? I remember thinking. Years later, as I began working as a therapist, I realized my client was likely experiencing something common on the path from unwell to well: a grief process that blindsides us because we don’t often recognize that healing, too, involves loss.

Source: iStock/Benjavisa

From Denial to Awareness

The path to healing looks different for everyone. It may include self-help books, journaling, a religious or spiritual practice, yoga, meditation, podcasts, therapy, or any combination of these.

Regardless of the path, we don’t always have the awareness and insight to articulate what, exactly, is wrong and why. What we may know is that we’re tired of not feeling good, and we want to feel better. For those who seek healing through therapy, the beginning often involves moving from denial (something is there, but I can't see it) to awareness (wow, now I see it).

This stage can feel exciting, like their world is being stretched in new ways. Clients become more aware of their thoughts, behaviors, and reactions. They realize they’re afraid of discomfort, and that they work very hard to avoid it.

Developing awareness is essential, but it’s not always enough to bring about change. We then start to peel back the layers, to explore the past with curiosity. Where do you suppose you learned that? What happened when you expressed emotions? What messages did you receive about your worth?

They start connecting the dots between the present and the past, between what they do and where they learned to do it. Awareness gives way to insight, and they move from wow, now I see it to now I understand why it's happening.

And while that insight may bring relief, it often leaves them looking back through a new lens, bringing more things into focus. Suddenly, unexpected emotions show up on the journey, blindsiding them in ways they never saw coming.

Anger

Exploring the past is not about blaming others for who we are, but rather about understanding who we became in light of others. It's about making sense of our story.

The problem is, when clients start to make sense of their own story, they begin to process what it cost them, and they find themselves feeling anger and resentment toward parents, family members, anyone they believe hurt them.

It’s not uncommon for clients to feel conflicted at this point, especially when the anger is directed at people they still love. Many worry it means they no longer care about the person, that they’re ungrateful, or that they’re betraying the relationship. As a result, they struggle to name it, let alone let themselves feel it.

So we work on learning to make room for it rather than judging it or pushing it away. The tricky part is that once they finally let themselves feel it, they want to take action. Suddenly, it's time to have the conversation, to confront the person, to get everything off their chest.

We shift our focus to learning to be with anger without letting it dictate what happens, because acting in anger will only keep wounds wide open. For many clients, this is incredibly hard. Not doing anything with their anger almost feels counterintuitive and unfair.

Viewing anger as part of the grief process that comes with healing helps them understand that anger is protecting them from the hurt underneath. They become less focused on getting rid of it and more willing to let it be. And as the anger loosens its grip, sadness emerges.

Sadness

Rarely do people move from anger to sadness overnight. More often, they experience both at the same time. This can be frustrating, especially for those who thought they had already "worked through" their anger.

But over time, they come to a tough realization: No amount of anger changes anything. The past remains the past, the loss is still the loss. And as that reality begins to settle in, sadness takes up all the space on the journey.

The source of sadness is unique to each person's story. Some grieve the parent they needed but didn't have. Others grieve years spent carrying responsibilities they didn't choose. Some grieve opportunities missed, dreams abandoned, or the life they imagined they would have.

But sometimes the sadness runs even deeper. Clients realize healing means letting go of an identity, of long-held beliefs, of all the ways they’ve been protecting themselves. Others start to see not only how they were wounded, but also how they have wounded others.

At times, clients can't pinpoint the source, but spending too much time trying to figure out the source can pull them away from the emotion itself, and this can prevent the wounds from healing. So we continue to work on letting them just feel it.

Acceptance

One of the questions clients ask me most often is, "How will I know when I'm healed?" It's a fair question.

Healing is not about never feeling sad, angry, or hurt again. It’s not about forgetting what happened or pretending it didn't matter. Healing looks like being able to look back at your story without being pulled under by it. It’s when the past remains the same, but it no longer emotionally hijacks you.

It’s also the point at which you stop waiting for someone to change, for someone to finally understand; you stop waiting for the apology, the acknowledgment, or the closure you may never receive.

And perhaps most importantly, it’s when you begin to see the humanity in everyone involved, including your own. You recognize people made choices that likely stemmed from their own wounds, their own limitations. And even though those choices caused pain, you realize you’re more than what happened to you.

item.title: Some Friendships Are Meant for a Chapter, Not a Lifetime
item.description:
Friends

Some Friendships Are Meant for a Chapter, Not a Lifetime

What workplace friendships teach us about letting go.

Posted June 20, 2026

Key points
  • Shared routines and repeated contact help create strong social bonds.
  • Major life transitions often weaken friendships by removing shared contexts.
  • The end of a friendship does not mean the relationship lacked meaning or significance.
  • Viewing some relationships as chapter friendships can reduce feelings of loss or failure.
Source: Ivan S / Pexels

I have been thinking recently about the many friendships I have formed through work. Having lived for work in both the United States and the United Kingdom, I am aware that expectations around friendship can vary across cultures. Some cultures place a stronger emphasis on maintaining lifelong social connections, while others may be more accepting of friendships that emerge around particular life circumstances.

Over the past five years, working in mental health services in the UK, I have formed many close friendships through work. Sharing long shifts, difficult situations, intense training, and emotionally demanding experiences can create a sense of connection that develops quickly and feels deeply meaningful.

Yet when people move roles, organisations, or locations, many of these friendships naturally fade. Looking back, I do not see them as failed friendships. Instead, I see them as relationships that were important for a particular period of my life—friendships that shaped a chapter, even if they were not meant to last a lifetime.

The Friendships That Shape Us

Chapter friendships appear throughout life. They may develop at university, during a first job, while raising young children, during a period of illness, or after moving to a new city.

Workplace friendships provide a particularly common example. We spend hours together, navigate challenges, celebrate successes, and support one another through stressful periods. Colleagues often know details about our daily lives that even long-term friends may not see.

Psychologists have long recognised that proximity plays an important role in relationship formation. The more frequently we encounter someone, the more likely we are to develop familiarity and connection (Zajonc, 1968). Shared experiences, goals, and routines further strengthen these bonds.

Over time, these friendships can feel deeply significant because they genuinely are.

Source: Meshack Emmanuel Kazanshyi / Pexels

When Life Turns the Page

The difficulty comes when the circumstances that created the friendship change.

A colleague moves to a different organisation. A university course ends. Children grow older. Someone relocates or enters a new life stage. The shared environment that once brought two people together disappears.

Sociologist Scott Feld (1981) argued that friendships are often organised around "social foci"—shared settings and activities that create opportunities for interaction. When those structures disappear, maintaining the relationship requires considerably more effort.

Sometimes friendships adapt and continue. Other times, they gradually fade.

The fading itself is often interpreted as evidence that the friendship was not genuine. In reality, the opposite may be true. The friendship may simply have fulfilled its role within a particular chapter of life.

Nostalgia Without Reconnection

Years later, we may think about these friends with genuine affection. We may smile when we hear their name or remember conversations that helped us through a difficult period. Yet we may feel little desire to reconnect.

This can seem strange. If the friendship mattered, shouldn't we want to revive it?

Not necessarily.

Research on nostalgia suggests that positive memories can provide comfort and meaning without creating a desire to recreate the past (Sedikides et al., 2008). We often miss the period of life as much as the person themselves.

The former colleague may remind us of our early career. The university friend may represent a time of possibility and exploration. The friendship becomes linked to a version of ourselves that no longer exists in quite the same way.

Why Letting Go Can Be Healthy

Social media has made it easier than ever to remain loosely connected to people from every stage of life. While this can be valuable, it has also reinforced the idea that meaningful relationships should be preserved indefinitely. Human relationships have rarely worked this way.

Throughout history, people have formed close bonds within communities, workplaces, schools, neighbourhoods, and shared experiences. Some relationships endured, while others naturally dissolved as people moved through different life stages.

Developmental research suggests that our personalities, priorities, and social needs continue to evolve throughout adulthood (Roberts et al., 2006). As we change, our relationships inevitably change too. Accepting this reality may help us move away from viewing every faded friendship as a loss.

Measuring Friendships Differently

Perhaps we need a different way of evaluating relationships. Rather than asking whether a friendship lasted forever, we might ask what role it played in our lives. Did it provide support during a difficult period? Did it help us grow? Did it offer companionship, laughter, or a sense of belonging when we needed it most?

If the answer is yes, then the friendship was successful.

Chapter friendships remind us that relationships do not need to be permanent to be meaningful. Some people walk beside us for a lifetime. Others accompany us for a few pages. Both can leave a lasting mark on who we become.

No AI tools were used to generate the content, ideas, analysis, or authorship of this article. AI-assisted software was used solely for minor grammar and spelling checks.

item.title: Ann Rule: From Ted Bundy’s Confidante to Crime Chronicler
item.description:
Career

Ann Rule: From Ted Bundy’s Confidante to Crime Chronicler

A new biography shows how writer Ann Rule became a “voice for victims.”

Posted June 20, 2026

Key points
  • True crime author Ann Rule called herself a psychological detective.
  • Her book on Ted Bundy launched her career and defined her style.
  • A new biography analyzes Rule’s development into a voice for crime victims.
Cathy Scott on Ann Rule's deck.
Source: With permission from Cathy Scott

In 2002, I interviewed Ann Rule, a bestselling true crime writer. Her first book in 1980, The Stranger Beside Me, featured her relationship with serial killer Ted Bundy, from working with him on a crisis hotline to supporting his claim of innocence to realizing he’d profoundly duped her.

Although she was best known for this association, she strove to shed it. She developed a full body of work and a unique approach that merits recognition. Journalist Cathy Scott’s unflinching new biography, First Lady of Murder, analyzes the late author's process.

Ann Rule’s Unique Writing Approach and Interview Style

Rule called herself a “psychological detective.” She’d learned from story immersion and empathic attunement how to make people feel heard. She developed her approach by watching detectives, attorneys, and courtroom personnel at work, and by visiting crime scenes and interviewing victims and perpetrators. Immersion allowed her to see a story from within and hook readers with her own emotional engagement. “I write it the way I live the story,” she said. “What fascinates me is a case where the truth is obscured from the beginning.”

“Ann Rule's interviews were semi-structured,” Scott told me. “Her questions were open-ended, meant to let the conversation drift. Calm and soft-spoken, she would recall events in passing to coax her interviewees into speaking freely. That same patience won over victims' families, who opened up to her.”

Scott, a long-time friend of Rule’s, used this same approach to listen for truths in Rule’s own story. She, too, is fascinated by what’s hidden.

Influence of Truman Capote and The Impact of Ted Bundy on Rule’s Career

During the mid-1960s, Rule had read Truman Capote's groundbreaking nonfiction novel, In Cold Blood, about two drifters who’d slaughtered a family in Kansas. She’d admired Capote’s rich narrative style and thought to herself, “If only I could get inside a killer's mind like that and find out what's going on, and then write a book, that's all I'd ever ask.” She certainly got that opportunity—and came to regret it. Her association with Bundy gave her writing career an enormous boost, but it also forced her onto an ethical tightrope and bound her to a killer she grew to detest.

There’s a lot in this biography about Bundy, and it’s not a glowing review of Rule’s approach. When she persistently supported his innocence, she overstepped with some detectives. She also made a devious deal with the killer yet convinced herself she’d been honest.

After he cut her off, she tried to re-engage him with money because the quality of her book depended on getting him to talk. It took her years to wake up. At Bundy’s Florida trial for the deadly Chi Omega attack, Rule finally heard evidence that clinched the cases against him. “I felt dumb,” she said. “I felt fooled, and I thought that my perception, which I'd always counted on, was flawed.”

It was a lesson that helped her with future books. Scott describes Rule’s ethical and narrative dilemmas within a compassionate context: Rule’s brother’s suicide. Perhaps Bundy was a brother substitute, Scott suggests, which might have biased her. Still, she made some serious missteps, and critics called her out.

Rule was especially intrigued with motive and mystery. “To her,” said Scott, “a killer was defined by the why, not the who. She [was] drawn to what makes a seemingly normal, nice person do monstrous things. Her subjects were ‘antiheroes,’ she said, attractive, brilliant, charming, admired, but hiding behind masks. Ugly killers held no interest for her. She admitted she did not write about them. She wanted someone who was ‘attractive, rich, brilliant, successful, charismatic.’ The gap between that public face and the private monster was what defined her.”

Before Bundy was even a suspect, however, Rule had wanted to write about the victims, the missing and murdered women of the Pacific Northwest. She was drawn to the broken places in people. She had told me, “I get more involved with the families of the victims than other writers. These people become friends while I'm writing and they stay friends. When I first began this work, I realized that someone had to die for me to make a living. I went to a psychiatrist and told him I really needed the job to support my children, but I wasn't sure that I could do it. He told me that half of the world makes a living off the other half's misfortune, and what matters is how you feel about those people. Then it was okay for me, because I knew that I really did care about them.” Scott says that Rule believed she helped them to get closure and she gave them a voice.

Cathy Scott’s Analysis of Ann Rule’s Writing Process and Legacy

Still, not all families thought Rule had been fair. As Scott writes, “It was the tension that had followed her throughout her career, the one she could never fully resolve, that fellow true-crime authors also, at times, faced: between a writer’s need to tell the story and a family’s need to own it.” Her successful authorship had its downside.

Rule had her secrets. She took some to the grave, but others are revealed in these pages. There’s a disturbing story from Bundy’s mother about how Rule, who lived close enough to visit, completely ignored her. Scott also includes comments from writers whom Rule burned or snubbed. She sometimes skirted etiquette, like paying her sources or undermining rivals, yet her considerable fan following is a testament to how much effort she put into her work.

Scott displays the layers of Rule’s writing life, dissecting the process of a woman who’d studied others in the same penetrating way. With Rule’s passing in 2015, her career is complete. Bundy remains her most defining crime association.

item.title: Spiritually Integrated Psychotherapy Across Cultures
item.description:
Spirituality

Spiritually Integrated Psychotherapy Across Cultures

Insights from Catholic therapists in Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America.

Posted June 20, 2026

Key points
  • Catholic therapists adapted spiritual interventions to fit the cultural values of their clients.
  • Catholic therapists frequently encouraged prayer, trust in God, and listening to the heart during treatment.
  • Clients experienced reductions in both spiritual and psychological distress during treatment.
  • Spiritual and psychological distress were closely intertwined throughout treatment.
St. Peter's Basilica and Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II bridge in Vatican City.
Source: Pajor Pawel/Shutterstock

Today, I share additional findings from the Enhancing Practice-Based Evidence for Spiritually Integrated Psychotherapies project. This post focuses on a study of Catholic therapists and clients in 13 countries by Wonjin Sim and her colleagues, published in the APA journal Psychotherapy (Sim et al., 2022). Their findings offer valuable insights for psychotherapists who wish to integrate faith and spirituality into their work. I thank Dr. Sim for her permission to share these findings.

The Research Study

The study examined the process and outcomes of spiritually integrated psychotherapies (SIPs) conducted by Catholic therapists in Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America. Although research on spiritually integrated psychotherapy has increased in recent years, most studies have been conducted in North America and with predominantly White Christian samples. This study provides insight into how SIPs are practiced internationally and whether they are associated with changes in clients' spiritual and nonspiritual distress.

Methods

The researchers used a practice-based evidence design rather than a randomized clinical trial. Therapists conducted therapy as they normally would, without a treatment manual or experimental manipulation. The study included 34 Catholic therapists practicing in 13 countries (Uganda, India, Korea, Mexico, Italy, Kenya, the Philippines, Malta, Vietnam, Myanmar, Belarus, the Czech Republic, and Colombia) and 359 clients who participated in 4,380 therapy sessions.

Most therapists were priests or nuns who had received training in spiritually integrated psychotherapy at the Pontifical Gregorian University’s Institute of Psychology in Rome or through alumni trained there. Of the 359 clients, 355 were Catholic, and 4 were Hindu. Clients presented with a wide range of concerns, including interpersonal conflict, self-esteem issues, trauma, personality disorders, and spiritual growth concerns.

The researchers assessed both spiritual and nonspiritual outcomes. Spiritual distress included concerns such as loss of spiritual direction or inspiration. Nonspiritual distress included psychological, relational, and physical health concerns. Therapists also completed a checklist after each session, identifying which spiritual interventions they had used.

Process Findings

Across all therapists and countries, the three most frequently used spiritual interventions were encouraging personal prayer, affirming trust in God, and encouraging clients to listen to their hearts. Other commonly used interventions included discussing hope, helping clients discern God's will, discussing self-control, exploring the spiritual dimensions of problems, encouraging acceptance of God's love, discussing gratitude, and using spiritual confrontation.

Therapists reported using at least one spiritual intervention in approximately 83 percent of all sessions. On average, therapists used about five spiritual interventions per session. Spiritual interventions were used more frequently during the early and middle phases of treatment than during the later phases. Therapists also tended to use more spiritual interventions with clients who reported higher levels of initial spiritual or nonspiritual distress.

The study found substantial differences in the types of spiritual interventions used across continents. In Africa, the most common interventions were encouraging personal prayer, affirming trust in God, and discussing hope. In Asia, the most common interventions were discussing self-control, discussing hope, and affirming trust in God. In Europe, therapists most frequently listened to spiritual issues, encouraged listening to the heart, and engaged in silent prayer. In Latin America, the most common interventions were spiritual confrontation, discussing the spiritual dimensions of problems and solutions, and spiritual self-disclosure. These differences provide evidence that the therapists adapted spiritually integrated psychotherapy to local cultural contexts.

Outcome Findings

Clients showed significant reductions in both spiritual and nonspiritual distress over the course of therapy. At intake, clients reported higher levels of spiritual distress, nonspiritual distress, and psychological symptoms than they did at the end of treatment. Growth-curve analyses indicated that improvement occurred most rapidly early in therapy and then continued at a slower rate as treatment progressed.

One of the study’s most intriguing findings concerned the relationship between spiritual distress and psychological distress. The two forms of distress were strongly correlated. Clients who experienced greater spiritual struggles also tended to report higher levels of emotional and psychological suffering. Likewise, when spiritual distress decreased, psychological distress often decreased as well.

However, the direction of change was somewhat unexpected. Improvements in psychological functioning during one therapy session predicted improvements in spiritual well-being during subsequent sessions. In contrast, improvements in spiritual well-being did not significantly predict later reductions in psychological symptoms.

The authors suggested that this pattern may reflect a developmental process. As emotional distress, anxiety, depression, or interpersonal conflict begin to improve, clients may become more capable of engaging spiritual questions and experiencing spiritual growth. In other words, psychological stabilization may create conditions that allow deeper spiritual healing to occur.

Conclusion

Spiritually integrated psychotherapies were associated with reductions in both spiritual and nonspiritual distress. Therapists may wish to use spiritual interventions with their clients, especially with those who value spirituality and who are experiencing spiritual distress. Therapists should use spiritual interventions based on clients' cultural and religious context and individual emotional and spiritual needs. Dr. Sim and her colleagues called for additional international research, including studies examining how therapists adapt spiritually integrated psychotherapy across different cultures and religious traditions. Investigations comparing SIPs with control conditions are also needed.

Psychotherapists seeking additional resources on integrating spirituality into treatment may find the publications in the references helpful, and other articles I have posted.
